messages.subject: DSM and stratification by year
parts:
Hi everyone

I am trying to use dsm in R to create density surface models of chimpanzee abundance. We used nest counts along transects and have two different survey years, I would like to see if there are any changes in abundance or distribution over time. When running the analysis in the Distance program we post-stratify by year, partly because we only have ~100 observations for each year (despite quite a large survey effort). My understanding is that you can't post-stratify in DSM.

My questions are:

1)Would it be ok to use Year as a covariate when defining the distance model? If it's not appropriate do I have any other options other than creating a ds model for each year? Perhaps just using Year in the GAM? or using a GAMM?

2) What happens with detection function covariates when you run the prediction? I can create a predictive surface of chimp density for the study site, but 'Year' is not included in the predictive data (and is not required), so i'm a little unsure what the surface I created represents.

Many thanks for any insights!

Cath

messages.author: 350dad0a615d36db
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] DSM and stratification by year
parts:
Hi Cath, hi listfolk,

In some sense DSM is a post-stratification, but in the sense that you
are explicitly modelling how density changes as a function of the
covariates, rather than defining areas over which to estimate density.

To your questions:

1) the question here is do you think that detectability changes by year?
If so, it's appropriate. If you wanted to use year as part of the
spatial model (either via a GAM or GAMM) you'd be saying that
distribution changes per year. A simple smooth of year really just
changes the level of the density over the whole area for that year --
it's not going to change spatial distribution within the year. You would
need to look at more complex models for that.

2) When covariates are used in the detection function they are included
in the fitted spatial model as an offset or as a correction to the count
(see Miller et al, 2013). Once the model is fitted, they play no part in
the prediction (as we've dealt with detectability by that point). The
surface you produce is averaging over years.



Hope this helps!

cheers,
--dave





References

Miller, D.L., Burt, M.L., Rexstad, E.A. and Thomas, L. (2013) Spatial
models for distance sampling data: recent developments and future
directions (ed O Gimenez). Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 4, 1001–1010.
